conversation.task: This is a fictional, low-stakes paper-story rehearsal. A hobby club has twenty minutes, three blank panels, scrap paper, and pencils to draft one understandable three-panel story display. A teammate says the first draft is confusing and proposes putting twelve narration slogans in its small opening panel. You think that panel will be hard to read. One imagined participant says a fast verbal explanation leaves them behind and asks for a written example. The group can try either a familiar lost-and-found story or a journey-home story; both are reversible paper sketches. The known downside is that trying a second story uses five of the twenty minutes. There is no evidence about which story the group prefers. Nobody has proposed a process. Reply in English in no more than 250 words. Include a short welcoming opening, your response to the proposal and concern, a comparison of feasible approaches with one usable example, and a usable plan for this bounded session. Treat all advice as provisional for the fictional group to choose; do not execute anything.
conversation.response:
Welcome—there’s time to make a clear sketch together, and a written example can give everyone something to refer to.

The twelve slogans might contain useful ideas, but I’m concerned they would crowd the small opening panel and make the story harder to follow. Could we keep them on scrap paper as candidate wording and try one short caption in the panel? The teammate may be noticing a real gap; it would help to identify what feels confusing before cutting or adding text.

For the participant who finds fast explanations difficult, we could provide a written three-panel outline and a quiet reading pause. Reading it aloud could be an optional supplement.

Two feasible approaches:

- Lost-and-found: a familiar setup may need little explanation. Example: Panel 1, “Mina finds a scarf.” Panel 2, “She asks whose it is.” Panel 3, “Its owner thanks her.” Draw the scarf in each panel to connect the actions.
- Journey home: a clear destination could connect the panels, though the route might need extra visual clues. A written outline would help here too.

Neither story has an established preference. A provisional twenty-minute plan: spend three minutes reading the example and gathering concerns, two choosing a story together, eight sketching, four checking whether the sequence makes sense, and three revising. Trying the other story would cost five minutes, so the group could explicitly choose that tradeoff if the first sketch remains unclear. These are suggestions for the group to adapt or reject.
